ocar.opportunity: Caenorhabditis elegans has a stereotyped neuron complement, consistent synaptic wiring, and a transparent body, so structure, synapses, and activity can be studied in identified cells of a complete nervous system.
ocar.challenge: Neuron identification, electron-microscopic connectivity, fluorescent synapse labeling, and whole-nervous-system calcium imaging have each advanced, and workers need an up-to-date methods synthesis rather than scattered protocols.
ocar.action: In a WormBook chapter in Genetics (2021), Emmons, Yemini, and Zimmer review fluorescent neuron identification, recommended EM connectomic methods, fluorescent probes for single synapses and connections, and microscopy plus genetically encoded Ca2+ indicators for activity in single neurons across the nervous system.
ocar.resolution: They argue these methods now support new C. elegans connectomic work, verification of EM reconstructions, experimental approaches to synapse formation, and observation of activity within single neurons nervous-system-wide.
ocar.future_work: They caution that globally expressed GECIs in cell bodies can miss or distort neurite-restricted Ca2+ signals unless compartmentalization is independently validated, and they point readers to recommended analysis pipelines such as Kaplan et al. (2018).

summaries.beginner: The tiny worm C. elegans is see-through and has a simple, stereotyped set of nerve cells. This methods chapter explains how to name those cells with fluorescent tags, map their connections, and watch them fire with calcium sensors.
summaries.intermediate: In Genetics (2021), Emmons, Yemini, and Zimmer survey methods for C. elegans nervous-system structure and activity. Transparency plus neuron-specific reporters allows identification in living animals; EM remains the gold standard for synaptic connectivity, now with more powerful techniques they recommend for new reconstructions. Fluorescent synapse probes verify EM maps and enable experiments on synapse formation, while Ca2+ imaging can report activity in single neurons across the entire nervous system. They also discuss limits of somatic GECI signals given thin neurites versus large cell-body volume.
summaries.advanced: This is a WormBook methods review, not a new connectome or activity atlas. The claim that activity can be observed across the entire nervous system describes capability opened by microscopy and GECIs, not a dataset released here. The selected extract warns against over-interpreting compartmentalized Ca2+ from globally expressed indicators without further validation (citing Liu et al. 2018b on AWA).

plain_language_summary: The tiny worm C. elegans is see-through and has a simple, stereotyped set of nerve cells. This methods chapter explains how to name those cells with fluorescent tags, map their connections, and watch them fire with calcium sensors.

ocar.opportunity: Credit assignment—deciding which of trillions of synapses to change after an outcome—is solved in machine learning by backpropagation, but biology lacks a plausible implementation of that algorithm.
ocar.challenge: A biologically workable alternative such as node perturbation needs circuit structures that inject exploratory variability, correlate it with reward, and assign credit locally; those structures had not been demonstrated anatomically in vertebrate basal ganglia.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv, Kornfeld, Wang, Januszewski, Fee, Denk and colleagues use automated connectomics on two volume-EM datasets of songbird Area X (j0126 and j0251, processed with SyConn2) plus a biophysical model. They test a node-perturbation-style reinforcement-learning architecture in which LMAN axons (exploratory variability) and HVC axons (song timing/context) should target different dendritic compartments of medium spiny neurons.
ocar.resolution: The predicted synaptic dichotomy holds: variability-encoding axons terminate predominantly on dendritic shafts, context-encoding axons predominantly on spines. The biophysical model built from the EM data suggests that this dichotomy facilitates efficient local credit assignment, which the authors present as strong evidence for a general basal-ganglia solution.
ocar.future_work: Code for the biophysical model is on GitHub; analysis code is promised upon final publication. The work is a preprint (this extract is the 27 October 2025 version of a 2020 posting) and does not claim that backpropagation is thereby ruled out in other circuits.

summaries.beginner: When a bird practices song, the brain must decide which tiny contacts to strengthen after a better or worse attempt. This study maps those contacts in a song-learning region and finds two kinds of incoming wires land on different parts of the same cells, which a model says could let learning happen locally.
summaries.intermediate: In a bioRxiv preprint, Kornfeld, Wang, Januszewski, Rother, Schubert, Goldman, Jain, Denk, and Fee reconstruct songbird Area X with automated volume EM and SyConn2, then test a node-perturbation model of reinforcement learning. LMAN axons that encode exploratory vocal variability terminate mainly on dendritic shafts of medium spiny neurons, while HVC axons that encode song timing terminate mainly on spines. A biophysical model using those morphologies argues that the shaft/spine split supports efficient local credit assignment, an alternative to backpropagation. Datasets are public on SyConn Web as j0126 and j0251.
summaries.advanced: The anatomical claim is a predominance of shaft versus spine targeting, not a numeric percentage in the selected text. The biophysical model uses specified conductances (for example g_NMDA = 0.2 nS, g_LMAN_MSN = 30 nS) and a plasticity threshold; those are modeling choices. “Strong evidence for a general, biologically plausible credit assignment model in vertebrate basal ganglia” is the authors’ interpretation of one specialized song-learning nucleus. Competing interest: JK holds shares of ariadne.ai ag.

plain_language_summary: When a bird practices song, the brain must decide which tiny contacts to strengthen after a better or worse attempt. This study maps those contacts in a song-learning region and finds two kinds of incoming wires land on different parts of the same cells, which a model says could let learning happen locally.

ocar.opportunity: A molecular model of a nervous system needs gene-expression maps at the same single-cell resolution as anatomy and wiring, which few animals can provide for every neuron.
ocar.challenge: Prior C. elegans profiling covered embryonic or early-larval stages only in part, and incomplete qualitative expression data had limited computational links from genes to the wiring diagram.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv (2020), Taylor, Santpere, Weinreb, Barrett, Reilly, Xu and colleagues (CeNGEN; Hammarlund, Hobert, Miller corresponding) produce expression profiles matching all 302 neurons of the mature C. elegans nervous system, with a thresholding approach for high-confidence per-type profiles, then computationally recover cis-regulatory motifs and adhesion-protein codes.
ocar.resolution: They report that neuron classes can be identified by combinatorial expression of specific gene families: each class expresses unique codes of about 23 neuropeptide-encoding genes and about 36 neuropeptide receptors, implying an expansive “wireless” network. Neuropeptide genes are among the most abundant detections, and even at the most stringent threshold each neuron expresses at least four neuropeptide-encoding genes. Data are at cengen.org and CengenApp.
ocar.future_work: They present the catalog as a foundation for experiments on gene regulation, process placement, and connectivity, including extending adhesion-code hypotheses to other gene families and neuron groups.

summaries.beginner: To understand how each worm nerve cell gets its identity, this team measured which genes are on in every one of the 302 neurons. The catalog shows each cell type has its own mix of chemical-messenger genes and points to DNA switches and sticky proteins that may help cells wire up.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2020 bioRxiv preprint, Taylor and colleagues report what they describe as the first transcriptome of every neuron type in an entire nervous system, complementing earlier partial embryonic and larval C. elegans profiles. Combinatorial codes in gene families distinguish classes; neuropeptide and receptor combinations (~23 and ~36 genes per class) suggest widespread extrasynaptic signaling conserved with reports in Hydra, Drosophila, and mouse cortex. Computational analyses identify cis-regulatory elements and adhesion proteins with potential roles in synaptic specificity and process placement. Transcription-factor families show distinct nervous-system patterns (T-box underrepresented; zinc finger broad; homeodomains tracking identity; nuclear hormone receptors enriched in sensory neurons).
summaries.advanced: The ~23/~36 figures are class-level unique codes as stated, not proof that those peptides form functional synapses. “At least four” neuropeptide genes per neuron is at the most stringent threshold examined. Adhesion codes “likely contribute” to neuropil formation; they are computational hypotheses. This extract is the December 2020 preprint, not a later journal version.

plain_language_summary: To understand how each worm nerve cell gets its identity, this team measured which genes are on in every one of the 302 neurons. The catalog shows each cell type has its own mix of chemical-messenger genes and points to DNA switches and sticky proteins that may help cells wire up.

ocar.opportunity: Large 3D EM reconstructions now contain thousands of neurons and millions of synapses, so automated morphological interpretation—including axon versus dendrite versus soma—is needed to read the connectome and to catch agglomeration mistakes.
ocar.challenge: Prior classifiers used hand-designed features plus organelles, or 2D projections in Cellular Morphology Networks, rather than the full 3D voxel neighborhood of a neurite.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv (2020), Li, Januszewski, Jain, and Li train 3D convolutional networks on voxels to label reconstructed fragments as axonal, dendritic, or somal, then use localized predictions to detect and correct inter-class merge errors, including soma-branch geometry sampled within the first 10 µm from the soma.
ocar.resolution: Mean F1 for subcompartment classification is 0.972, above a previous state of the art of 0.955. Combined branch and soma merge analyses detect 90.6% of inter-class merge errors at a 2.7% false-positive rate. Soma-near branch classification reaches F1 0.923 at slope 0.78.
ocar.future_work: They expect finer-grained labels (spine versus shaft versus AIS) and neuronal subtype identification, and they note that processing efficiency falls as field of view grows because the neurite occupies a shrinking voxel fraction—mitigable with sparse 3D representations.

summaries.beginner: Computers that glue bits of nerve cells together sometimes fuse an axon onto a dendrite by mistake. This method looks at the 3D shape of each bit, labels it as axon, dendrite, or cell body, and uses those labels to find and cut many of those bad fusions.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2020 bioRxiv paper, Li, Januszewski, Jain, and Li introduce voxel-based 3D CNNs for axon/dendrite/soma classification of reconstructed neuron fragments, exceeding CMN-style 2D projection methods (mean F1 0.972 versus 0.955). Fine localization of those labels supports automated merge-error detection and correction: 90.6% of inter-class merges found at 2.7% false positives. Best soma-exit branch performance uses skeleton nodes in the first 10 µm from the soma. Training data and the EM volume were shared by Schubert and Kornfeld.
summaries.advanced: Metrics are for inter-class merges and the reported test setting, not all merge types. The 0.955 comparator is the previous CMN state of the art they cite, not a multi-challenge leaderboard. Efficiency versus field of view is an explicit limitation. Organism is not named in the abstract; the volume acknowledgment points at songbird EM used with CMN.

plain_language_summary: Computers that glue bits of nerve cells together sometimes fuse an axon onto a dendrite by mistake. This method looks at the 3D shape of each bit, labels it as axon, dendrite, or cell body, and uses those labels to find and cut many of those bad fusions.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomic EM volumes are mosaics of thousands to millions of overlapping 2D tiles that must be registered into one coherent stack before segmentation or tracing.
ocar.challenge: Existing deformation solvers were inadequate for the largest volumes and inefficient even for small jobs, and a least-squares system without a usable regularization prior cannot be applied beyond trivial cases.
ocar.action: In an April 2018 arXiv paper, Khairy, Denisov, and Saalfeld formulate joint deformable registration as a linear system that minimizes feature-pair square distances with explicit constraints, constructing a rigid-model approximation as prior when none is available, then delegate the solve to standard linear-algebra packages (direct methods, including PaStiX for systems with more than one million tiles).
ocar.resolution: They jointly align 2.67 million images with more than 200 million point-pairs and report successful alignment of the first full adult fruit fly brain (FAFB). Direct solvers outperform iterative ones on time, residual error, and precision in their tests; a λ sweep on a 536-tile montage shows the deformation–prior tradeoff.
ocar.future_work: They present the matrix formulation as decoupling EM registration from solver engineering so future scalable linear solvers apply automatically; Matlab code estimates translation, rigid, affine, and polynomial (up to third degree) models.

summaries.beginner: A whole fly brain is photographed as millions of slightly overlapping snapshots that must be stitched and stacked without tearing the tissue digitally. This paper turns that puzzle into a large math problem a standard linear solver can handle, and uses it on the first complete adult fruit-fly brain volume.
summaries.intermediate: On arXiv (2018), Khairy, Denisov, and Saalfeld describe a matrix-based solver for montage, rough, and fine alignment of serial-section EM. The system combines point-match residuals with regularization; a rigid-model approximation supplies a prior. They apply it to 2.67 million images and more than 200 million point-pairs for FAFB. Intro scale context: imaging a ~500 µm fly brain at 4×4×40 nm³ with 10% tile overlap would generate about 21 million images. On a 32-CPU Broadwell node, direct methods beat iterative ones; PaStiX excelled above 1 million tiles.
summaries.advanced: “Successfully aligning the first full adult fruit fly brain” credits this solver’s use on FAFB; residual error tables are summarized qualitatively in the extract. Hardware timings are for their Matlab/PaStiX setup, not a multi-package bakeoff of all EM aligners. The ~21 million image figure is an illustrative whole-brain acquisition estimate from Zheng et al. 2017, not the 2.67 million they jointly solved.

plain_language_summary: A whole fly brain is photographed as millions of slightly overlapping snapshots that must be stitched and stacked without tearing the tissue digitally. This paper turns that puzzle into a large math problem a standard linear solver can handle, and uses it on the first complete adult fruit-fly brain volume.

ocar.opportunity: Electrical synapses help define how a nervous system processes information, but unlike chemical synapses they are hard to map in high-throughput EM, so an “electrical connectome” is missing for most animals.
ocar.challenge: Even in C. elegans only a single adult hermaphrodite chemical connectome had been fully reconstructed, which blocks nervous-system-wide views of how gap junctions change with environment or state.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv (2018), Bhattacharya, Aghayeva, Berghoff, and Hobert map genome-wide innexin expression across the nervous system, then track how those codes change in the dauer diapause, combine that with dauer locomotion and chemosensory assays, and dissect intersectional regulation by terminal selectors and FoxO.
ocar.resolution: Fourteen of 25 innexin genes are expressed in complex neuronal codes; 12 of those 14 change in a neuron-type-specific way in dauer, affecting 86 of 118 neuron classes, and non-neuronal inx-6 turns on in the dauer nervous system. ASK and RIM express up to 11 innexins; I6 expresses one. Remodeling of identified electrical synapses accounts for aspects of dauer locomotion and chemosensation; upregulation of inx-6 in AIB generates novel electrical connections.
ocar.future_work: They hypothesize that combinatorial innexin codes specify partners and synapse-specific conductance, including possible directionality. Full EM reconstruction of the dauer electrical connectome is noted as still needed to see partner gain and loss versus composition change at existing contacts.

summaries.beginner: Worms can change how their nerve cells are electrically coupled when they enter a hardy “dauer” state. This study maps which gap-junction proteins each neuron makes, shows those recipes change in most cell types in dauer, and links some of those changes to crawling and smell.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2018 bioRxiv preprint, Bhattacharya, Aghayeva, Berghoff, and Hobert treat innexin expression as a proxy for the C. elegans electrical connectome. Fourteen innexins form combinatorial neuronal codes that are not static: dauer entry alters 12 of 14 neuronal innexins across 86 of 118 classes, with isoform-specific and on/off flips, plus inx-6 induction. An intersectional terminal-selector plus FoxO mechanism explains neuron-type- and environment-specific changes. Functional tests of individual electrical synapses tie remodeling to dauer locomotion and chemosensory behavior, including new AIB connections via inx-6.
summaries.advanced: Innexin expression is not the same as an EM gap-junction map; the authors emphasize EM’s difficulty detecting electrical synapses. Partner changes versus conductance changes at existing contacts are both possible and only partly resolved (inx-6 in AIB is a gain-of-connection example). Dauer is one environmental trajectory, not all plasticity. This is the 31 August 2018 preprint.

plain_language_summary: Worms can change how their nerve cells are electrically coupled when they enter a hardy “dauer” state. This study maps which gap-junction proteins each neuron makes, shows those recipes change in most cell types in dauer, and links some of those changes to crawling and smell.

ocar.opportunity: Deep networks have been reported to segment neurons from serial EM at “super-human” accuracy, which could make connectomics usable far beyond the labs that collect each volume.
ocar.challenge: Those algorithms, the authors argue, do not generalize beyond the source and tissue they were trained on, so the broader neuroscience community still cannot apply them off the shelf.
ocar.action: On arXiv (2018, this extract v4 January 2020), Linsley, Kim, Berson, and Serre introduce the STAR challenge (source- and tissue-agnostic reconstruction of neurons), show that current state-of-the-art segmenters perform poorly on it, and propose fGRU, a convolutional recurrent module with short-range horizontal connections plus long-range top-down feedback that they contrast with hGRU’s strained horizontal dynamics.
ocar.resolution: fGRU establishes state of the art on STAR and is presented as a step toward widely usable, fully automated connectomics. The paper also cites a reported 250-fold reduction in processing time versus brute-force manual annotation for a 100³ µm³ volume from prior work, while arguing the field should shift from volume-specific fitting to cross-volume generalization.
ocar.future_work: They hope STAR and fGRU become building blocks for generalization-focused connectomic vision rather than dataset-specific leaderboard fitting.

summaries.beginner: Computer programs that outline nerve cells in electron-microscope pictures often work well only on the pictures they were trained on. This paper sets a harder test that mixes sources and tissues, shows leading methods stumble, and offers a new network that does better on that test.
summaries.intermediate: In an arXiv computer-vision paper, Linsley, Kim, Berson, and Serre argue that published super-human EM neuron segmentation does not transfer across imaging sources and tissues. They define STAR to favor generalization, document poor SOTA transfer, and introduce fGRU, which gates horizontal interactions with top-down feedback to suppress pathological dynamics seen in a single hGRU layer. fGRU is reported as STAR state of the art. The work is framed as shifting emphasis from fitting one volume to generalizing across volumes.
summaries.advanced: STAR results are the authors’ challenge, not a community bakeoff with independent organizers in this extract. The 250-fold speedup is cited from other work [18], not measured here. “Fully automated connectomics” is a stated direction, not a claim that proofreading is obsolete. No numeric STAR scores appear in the selected text.

plain_language_summary: Computer programs that outline nerve cells in electron-microscope pictures often work well only on the pictures they were trained on. This paper sets a harder test that mixes sources and tissues, shows leading methods stumble, and offers a new network that does better on that test.

ocar.opportunity: Automated EM segmentation must handle merge errors, which humans spot from overall neuronal shape even when local membrane classification looks fine.
ocar.challenge: Neurons sprout highly variable branches, so correct morphology cannot be catalogued, and merge errors take many forms; existing connectomics nets emphasize local boundary classification rather than high-level shape.
ocar.action: In a 2017 arXiv paper, Rolnick, Meirovitch, Parag, Pfister, Jain, Lichtman, Boyden, and Shavit introduce MergeNet: a 3D ConvNet trained without supervision to detect merge errors from morphology alone, ignoring the raw image at inference in the “zoom out” regime they describe, and they also test on merged MNIST digits.
ocar.resolution: MergeNet generalizes without retraining across connectomics datasets, can flag errors inside its own training set, and enables automatic comparison of segmentation methods and pipeline integration without extra annotation. It localizes merges (including some parallel-touch cases) but does not by itself correct them.
ocar.future_work: Exact automatic cuts would need the microscope image or membrane probabilities, because morphology often cannot say which continuation is which after a contact or how to split multi-object tangles. They sketch morphology-based typing and anomaly detection as longer-term uses.

summaries.beginner: When a computer accidentally glues two nerve cells into one, people can often see that the shape looks wrong. This network learns that kind of shape sense without extra hand labels and can flag glued cells in new datasets, though it cannot always cut them apart by itself.
summaries.intermediate: On arXiv (2017), Rolnick and colleagues show that 3D ConvNets can detect merge errors from neuronal morphology. MergeNet is trained unsupervised, operates across datasets without retraining, and is also demonstrated on a merged-MNIST control. The authors stress that merges, not only splits, are a central remaining barrier given millimeter-scale path lengths versus zettabyte-scale human-brain imaging estimates they cite. Failure modes include coincident branch points that resemble crosses and parallel processes without morphological clues at some boundary locations.
summaries.advanced: No numeric precision/recall on named EM volumes appears in the selected extract. The zettabyte human-brain figure is an estimate they cite [17], not a result. MergeNet detects and localizes; correction is explicitly out of scope. Unsupervised training does not mean the method needs no segmented objects—it uses existing segmentations without extra merge labels.

plain_language_summary: When a computer accidentally glues two nerve cells into one, people can often see that the shape looks wrong. This network learns that kind of shape sense without extra hand labels and can flag glued cells in new datasets, though it cannot always cut them apart by itself.

ocar.opportunity: Nanometer-scale EM volumes used to reconstruct wiring diagrams are often hundreds of terabytes and must be segmented for cell boundaries, synapses, and organelles.
ocar.challenge: Segmentation of a single volume is complex, time-intensive, and spread across a diverse tool set and many users, which makes it hard to track state, progress, provenance, and accountability.
ocar.action: In IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (2016), Al-Awami, Beyer, Haehn, Kasthuri, Lichtman, Pfister, and Hadwiger present NeuroBlocks, a multi-user web application designed from a domain-task analysis to integrate manual and semi-automatic segmentation, proofreading, visualization, and analysis tools used in large connectomics projects.
ocar.resolution: They describe NeuroBlocks as the first system that integrates this heterogeneous tool set with support for management, provenance, accountability, and auditing of large-scale segmentations, and they demonstrate the design in two case studies with different user roles in a real-world project.
ocar.future_work: The paper is a visualization-system design study; broader adoption and quantitative throughput gains versus prior lab practice are left to those case studies and later use rather than a public benchmark in the abstract.

summaries.beginner: When many people edit a giant brain-map project with different computer programs, it is easy to lose track of what is done and who changed what. This paper describes a shared website that follows segmentation and proofreading progress across those tools.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE TVCG (2016), Al-Awami, Beyer, Haehn, Kasthuri, Lichtman, Pfister, and Hadwiger introduce NeuroBlocks for tracking the state, progress, and evolution of very large volumetric neuroscience segmentations. After analyzing domain tasks, they abstract a visual representation and a web-based multi-user workflow that sits over existing manual and semi-automatic segmentation, proofreading, visualization, and analysis software. Two case studies address different user roles in a large real-world connectomics project. Volumes are described as often hundreds of terabytes.
summaries.advanced: The attached PDF extract does not match this catalog record: it is SynAnno (Lauenburg et al., 2025 bioRxiv), a later synapse-proofreading tool. Summaries here follow the NeuroBlocks abstract only. No numeric user-study timings or error rates appear in that abstract. “First system” is the authors’ integration claim.

plain_language_summary: When many people edit a giant brain-map project with different computer programs, it is easy to lose track of what is done and who changed what. This paper describes a shared website that follows segmentation and proofreading progress across those tools.

ocar.opportunity: Resurgent interest in synaptic circuitry and plasticity needs densely reconstructed hippocampal neuropil that can train people, constrain biophysical models, and test reconstruction algorithms.
ocar.challenge: Prior 3DEM of hippocampus had not provided densely reconstructed public volumes with all axons, dendrites, glia, and synapses, plus traces and software, at a resolution that also captures subcellular organelles.
ocar.action: In Scientific Data (2015), Harris, Spacek, Bell, Parker, Lindsey, Baden, Vogelstein, and Burns release three adult-rat CA1 neuropil volumes imaged at about 2 nm in X–Y on 50–60 nm serial sections, densely reconstructed in a cube (~10 µm³) around a large spine, a cylinder (~43 µm³) around a 3.4 µm oblique dendrite, and a parallelepiped (~178 µm³) around a 4.9 µm apical dendrite, hosted with Reconstruct files at the Open Connectome Project.
ocar.resolution: These are presented as the first densely reconstructed hippocampal volumes, with quantified synapses from varying section planes and reconstructions of microtubules, polyribosomes, SER, and endosomes in a subset of dendrites, intended as ultrastructural standards, modeling geometry, and a segmentation test bed.
ocar.future_work: They flag extracellular-space underestimation from oblique membranes and chemical fixation, alignment scaling of about 10–15% on average in Reconstruct for the apical and oblique volumes, and they hope the data seed machine-learning detection of rare objects such as the spine apparatus and studies of learning and disease.

summaries.beginner: This paper shares three tiny but complete 3D electron-microscope maps of rat hippocampus, with every axon, dendrite, glial bit, and synapse traced. Students and computer programs can use them as a practice set for reading brain ultrastructure.
summaries.intermediate: In Scientific Data (2015), Harris and colleagues publish three densely reconstructed adult-rat CA1 volumes at ~2 nm X–Y and ~50–60 nm section thickness: ~10, ~43, and ~178 µm³ around a large spine, an oblique dendrite, and an apical dendrite. All axons, dendrites, glia, and synapses are reconstructed; representative subcellular organelles are traced in a subset of dendrites. Images, traces, and Reconstruct software are freely available via the Open Connectome Project. Alignment in Reconstruct required on average ~10–15% overall scaling for the apical and oblique volumes, concentrated away from the densely reconstructed centers.
summaries.advanced: “First densely reconstructed hippocampal volumes” is the authors’ claim. ECS measurements are qualified by oblique-section occlusion and fixation/dehydration effects versus cryo-EM. Scaling artifacts are largest at image edges; dense reconstructions were kept near center. Organism is Rattus norvegicus hippocampal formation.

plain_language_summary: This paper shares three tiny but complete 3D electron-microscope maps of rat hippocampus, with every axon, dendrite, glial bit, and synapse traced. Students and computer programs can use them as a practice set for reading brain ultrastructure.

ocar.opportunity: Serial-section electron microscopy and other high-throughput imaging produce more than a terabyte per day, which individual lab workstations cannot store or analyze while building connectomes.
ocar.challenge: The community needed a shared, spatially indexed cluster that could run computer-vision pipelines in parallel, keep some products private, and still follow open-science sharing for the images.
ocar.action: At SSDBM (2013), Burns, Gray Roncal, Kleissas, Lillaney, Vogelstein and colleagues describe the Open Connectome Project data cluster: spatial-index partitioning across nodes, reads to parallel disk arrays and writes to solid-state storage, and stateless RESTful web services, publicly at openconnecto.me, with a production performance evaluation.
ocar.resolution: OCP offers storage and analysis services in exchange for contributed imaging data, modeled on Sloan Digital Sky Survey open science. The authors report that leading groups had already deposited the largest image stack and the most detailed neural reconstruction then managed by the project, and they highlight effective spatial data organization.
ocar.future_work: The design is aimed at 3D EM first but also time-series and multi-channel data; scaling the same architecture as volumes grow further is the implied operational agenda.

summaries.beginner: Brain microscopes now generate more pictures than a single lab computer can hold. This paper describes a shared computer cluster and web services that store those pictures, run analysis jobs, and let scientists work through the internet.
summaries.intermediate: In the 2013 International Conference on Statistical and Scientific Database Management (arXiv:1306.3543), Burns, Gray Roncal, and colleagues present the Open Connectome Project cluster for spatial analysis and annotation of high-throughput brain imaging, initially 3D EM. Data are partitioned by spatial index, I/O is split so reads hit disk arrays and writes hit SSDs, and all APIs are REST. The system targets connectome workloads via parallel vision on HPC clusters, includes a production performance evaluation, and serves data at openconnecto.me.
summaries.advanced: Performance claims in the selected text are qualitative (“highlighting effectiveness of spatial data organization”); numeric throughputs are not in this excerpt. “Largest image stack” and “most detailed neural reconstruction” refer to holdings at the time, cited to other papers. Catalog year is 2013 conference; this extract is the arXiv v2 text.

plain_language_summary: Brain microscopes now generate more pictures than a single lab computer can hold. This paper describes a shared computer cluster and web services that store those pictures, run analysis jobs, and let scientists work through the internet.

ocar.opportunity: Cortical function depends on synaptic wiring diagrams, but a full EM reconstruction of a cortical column was then impossible, so connectivity has to be described statistically from sampled recordings.
ocar.challenge: Pair recordings had shown sparse, often bidirectional-overrepresented connectivity and broad strength distributions, yet motifs beyond two neurons, the shape of the strength distribution, and correlations among strengths sharing a cell were open.
ocar.action: In PLoS Biology (2005), Song, Sjöström, Reigl, Nelson, and Chklovskii analyze several hundred simultaneous quadruple whole-cell recordings from layer 5 pyramidal neurons in rat visual cortex, counting two- and three-neuron motifs and measuring peak EPSP amplitudes.
ocar.resolution: Bidirectional connections are overrepresented versus random; several clustered three-neuron patterns are overrepresented. Connection strengths differ from Poisson and fit a lognormal, concentrating weight in a heavy tail; strengths sharing pre- or postsynaptic neurons are correlated, so strong connections cluster even more. They summarize the local network as a skeleton of stronger connections in a sea of weaker ones.
ocar.future_work: They argue that skeleton is likely important for network dynamics and should be investigated further; existing data were still insufficient for scale-free or small-world tests they discuss in the introduction.

summaries.beginner: Are local brain circuits just random spaghetti, or do they have a hidden pattern? Recordings from groups of rat visual-cortex cells show extra two-way links, extra triangles, and a few very strong contacts that tend to hang together—more like a sturdy skeleton than a uniform mesh.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS Biology (2005), Song, Sjöström, Reigl, Nelson, and Chklovskii probe layer 5 pyramids in rat visual cortex with quadruple whole-cell recordings. Relative to random graphs, bidirectional pairs and several clustered three-cell motifs are overrepresented. EPSP amplitudes follow a lognormal rather than Poisson distribution, implying synaptic weight is concentrated in few connections, and amplitudes are correlated among connections that share a pre- or postsynaptic cell. Overrepresentation of bidirectional motifs increases when a higher strength threshold is applied. The proposed picture is a skeleton of strong synapses among many weak ones.
summaries.advanced: This is electrophysiological sampling, not an EM connectome; “several hundred” quadruples is the scale given, not a complete column. Lognormal is a fit they report versus Poisson, not versus every alternative. Organism is rat visual cortex. Dynamics of the skeleton are inferred, not simulated in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Are local brain circuits just random spaghetti, or do they have a hidden pattern? Recordings from groups of rat visual-cortex cells show extra two-way links, extra triangles, and a few very strong contacts that tend to hang together—more like a sturdy skeleton than a uniform mesh.

ocar.opportunity: Dense EM connectomes such as FlyWire reconstruct hundreds of thousands of neurons, creating a chance to learn compact representations that combine morphology and wiring with little manual labeling.
ocar.challenge: Downstream analyses still often depend on predefined types, curated partner labels, and expert clustering, and coarse skeletons can discard identity information while geometry can confound developmental variation.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv (2026), Shi, Chen, Liu, and Zhang train a hierarchical graph neural network with skeleton decomposition for contrastive learning on finely sampled FlyWire skeletons (v630 SWCs; synapses from v783), then use structural embeddings as continuous partner descriptors and iterate multi-hop connectivity learning, with attention to interpret partners.
ocar.resolution: Fine skeletons preserve richer identity than coarse ones, and coordinate-free topology reduces geometric confounds while improving clustering and label-efficient inference. Structure-driven connectivity representations improve subtype discrimination without predefined partner-type labels, and multi-hop learning reveals hemispheric lateralization and connectivity-defined subgroups. They treat this as a self-supervised framework for discovering organization beyond canonical labels.
ocar.future_work: They list limits: adding transcriptomic, functional, or developmental modalities; jointly clustering structural and multi-hop views; treating attention cautiously pending perturbation/ablation; and validating on other connectomes and populations.

summaries.beginner: A whole-fly wiring map is so big that people cannot sort every cell by hand. This study trains a computer to learn each cell’s shape and who it talks to from the FlyWire map, then uses those learned fingerprints to find groups that standard name tags miss.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2026 bioRxiv preprint, Shi, Chen, Liu, and Zhang present self-supervised structure–connectivity learning on the FlyWire whole-brain connectome. A hierarchical GNN with skeleton decomposition is trained contrastively on fine skeletons; coordinate-free topology is reported to improve clustering and label-efficient inference versus geometry-confounded features. Learned embeddings then describe synaptic partners continuously, improving subtype discrimination (experiments include Kenyon-cell subtypes and optic Tm types) without predefined partner-type labels. Iterative multi-hop learning and attention analysis surface higher-order organization including hemispheric connectivity lateralization.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods preprint on FlyWire releases v630 (skeletons, taxonomy) and v783 (synapses), not a new EM volume. “Substantially richer identity” is qualitative in the abstract. Attention links are explicitly to be validated by perturbation. Supervised KC experiments use 12 subtype classes listed in methods; those labels still come from FlyWire tables even when partner types are not predefined.

plain_language_summary: A whole-fly wiring map is so big that people cannot sort every cell by hand. This study trains a computer to learn each cell’s shape and who it talks to from the FlyWire map, then uses those learned fingerprints to find groups that standard name tags miss.

ocar.opportunity: Post-embryonic remodeling of a complete synaptic connectome can show how a brain’s mesoscopic core is built while behavior remains possible, which C. elegans uniquely allows.
ocar.challenge: How edge density, hierarchy, rich-club structure, and hub identity change from hatching through larval stages—and whether the core is a fixed set of neurons—was not mapped on the developing worm “brain” network they study.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv (2026), Yadav and Singh analyze the developing C. elegans brain connectome across post-embryonic stages, tracking edge density, weak connectivity, k-core and rich-club organization, and persistence versus turnover of core neurons, in light of previously reported asymmetric synapse addition.
ocar.resolution: Starting with most head neurons already present at hatching, the network adds many synapses and raises edge density while remaining weakly connected. The core has a conserved persistent backbone plus transient or recurring neurons. Rich-club organization exists from the early stage and selectively strengthens among integrators, while input hubs are preserved and the in-degree k-core becomes more centralized.
ocar.future_work: They present the work as a perspective on neurodevelopment that may inform function; comparative tests across taxa are motivated in the introduction rather than executed here.

summaries.beginner: Even a tiny worm brain keeps growing new connections after hatching. This study watches that wiring over larval life and finds a stable inner club of cells plus some members that come and go, while the club’s links get denser.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2026 bioRxiv preprint, Yadav and Singh study post-embryonic development of the C. elegans brain connectome (they describe a brain of around 200 neurons). Edge density increases while weak connectivity is maintained. At mesoscale, the core mixes persistent neurons with transient or recurring ones. A rich club is present early and strengthens, consistent with asymmetric synapse addition among integrators; input hubs persist and the in-degree k-core centralizes. The authors frame this as developmental continuity of core organization rather than wholesale replacement.
summaries.advanced: “Around 200 neurons” refers to their head/brain subgraph, not the classic 302-neuron whole-animal count. Rich-club strengthening is interpreted via previously reported asymmetric synapse addition, not a new EM reconstruction in this paper. The selected extract’s back half is mostly methods references; quantitative tables are not in the provided text. This is a preprint.

plain_language_summary: Even a tiny worm brain keeps growing new connections after hatching. This study watches that wiring over larval life and finds a stable inner club of cells plus some members that come and go, while the club’s links get denser.

ocar.opportunity: After vEM acquisition, millions of tiles must be montaged and aligned into a coherent volume; even subtle misregistration undermines automatic segmentation and all downstream connectomics.
ocar.challenge: Classical stitchers and spring-mesh aligners oversimplify deformations and fail at tears, folds, and wrinkles, while deep-learning aligners add training cost and black-box behavior, and few tools integrate 2D stitching with 3D alignment in a lightweight package.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv (2026), Wu and Lichtman introduce FEABAS (Finite-Element Assisted Brain Assembly System), an open-source Python workflow that uses adaptive meshes and finite-element analysis to elastically montage and align serial EM, concentrating degrees of freedom at artifact “kink points” and solving static equilibrium as a sparse linear system.
ocar.resolution: FEABAS is presented as robust to wrinkles, folds, tears, and broken sections, scalable and cross-platform, with interpretable stress/strain diagnostics and error distributed across z rather than accumulated against a fixed reference. It requires material masks for artifacts, which can be manual or delegated to segmentation networks.
ocar.future_work: They argue decoupling semantic masking from geometric registration lets labs swap in better defect detectors without changing the solver; generating masks for subtle artifacts remains a practical bottleneck they acknowledge.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope pictures of brain slices often wrinkle, tear, or fold, which makes stacking them into a 3D volume hard. This free software treats the stack like a physical mesh and stretches it smoothly around those defects instead of forcing a simple warp.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2026 bioRxiv preprint, Wu and Lichtman describe FEABAS for elastic 2D stitching and 3D alignment of serial EM. Adaptive finite-element meshes capture non-smooth artifacts that interpolation and regular-grid spring models miss; equilibrium is solved globally as a sparse linear system rather than by slow transient simulation. They contrast this with deep-learning registration’s training overhead and with sequential z-alignment’s drift. A 1 mm³ volume is cited as easily exceeding 100 million tiles given limited fields of view. Artifact masks are an operational requirement.
summaries.advanced: No numeric residual-error tables appear in the selected text. Robustness to named artifacts is a design claim illustrated in the discussion, not a public leaderboard score here. Masking effort can dominate for large dirty datasets. Catalog stages include graph analysis; the paper itself is alignment infrastructure.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope pictures of brain slices often wrinkle, tear, or fold, which makes stacking them into a 3D volume hard. This free software treats the stack like a physical mesh and stretches it smoothly around those defects instead of forcing a simple warp.

ocar.opportunity: Volume EM is often highly anisotropic—fine in x–y, coarse in z—which blurs membranes in xz/yz and hurts segmentation and connectomic tracing, while interpolating missing slices cannot restore unacquired high-frequency structure.
ocar.challenge: Learning-based isotropic reconstruction can hallucinate implausible textures or jump between slices unless it has domain-consistent perceptual priors and explicit cross-slice consistency; labeled isotropic volumes are scarce.
ocar.action: In Electronics (2026), Qiu, Wan, Zhou, Liao, Liu, Li, and Du pretrain a vision transformer with DINOv3 student–teacher self-distillation on high-resolution xy sections, then train a conditional diffusion denoiser on simulated z-downsampling with a frozen-ViT perceptual loss.
ocar.resolution: On two public vEM datasets they report improved fidelity, perceptual quality, and membrane-boundary continuity versus interpolation and learning-based baselines, with fewer hallucinated textures and less inter-slice drift.
ocar.future_work: The framework still depends on simulating anisotropy by z-downsampling of existing stacks rather than new physical sections; how well it transfers to other modalities and real section-thickness blur is the natural next test.

summaries.beginner: Many 3D electron-microscope stacks are sharp from above but blurry when viewed from the side because slices are thick. This method teaches a generative model what real thin slices look like, then invents the missing in-between slices more cleanly than simple stretching.
summaries.intermediate: In Electronics (2026), Qiu and colleagues propose two-stage cross-axial super-resolution for anisotropic vEM. DINOv3-style self-distillation on abundant xy sections yields vEM-specific ViT features; a conditional diffusion model is trained with supervised z-downsampling plus perceptual loss on frozen ViT distances. They motivate the problem with typical 3–5 nm xy pixels versus 30–70 nm z sampling (about 6–20× coarser axially) for ssTEM/SBF-SEM. Experiments on two public datasets claim better fidelity, perceptual scores, and membrane continuity than interpolation and prior learning methods.
summaries.advanced: Dataset names and numeric PSNR/SSIM-style scores are not in the selected extract. Anisotropy figures (3–5 nm vs 30–70 nm; 6–20×) are typical ranges in the introduction, not measurements of the two test sets. Super-resolution can still hallucinate; the paper argues their priors reduce that risk. FIB-SEM can already be near-isotropic but is described as limited in volume and cost.

plain_language_summary: Many 3D electron-microscope stacks are sharp from above but blurry when viewed from the side because slices are thick. This method teaches a generative model what real thin slices look like, then invents the missing in-between slices more cleanly than simple stretching.

ocar.opportunity: Neuroimaging shows large-scale functional network remodeling in development and after injury, which would be a powerful substrate for recovery if the microscopic mechanisms were known.
ocar.challenge: Growth of entirely new long-distance axons in adult brains is unlikely, so it has been unclear how long-range network plasticity could occur without new cables.
ocar.action: In Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2026), Richards, Huang, Bauer, and Lee synthesize EM connectome and single-cell projectome evidence across model organisms on highly arborized long-range axons, branch-specific myelination, and axonal territories with few synaptic contacts that might still form new synapses, including after focal injury.
ocar.resolution: They propose that these conserved axonal features could implement long-range functional plasticity by recruiting additional branches and areas rather than growing wholly new axons, linking synaptic, single-neuron, and network scales. They also note differential myelination and branch-specific spike propagation as ways one axon could influence targets unequally.
ocar.future_work: How “silent” or sparsely synapsing branches persist instead of being pruned remains open; they argue that understanding branch construction and maintenance will matter for promoting plasticity after stroke and developmental lesions. Recovery differences among patients are offered as a possible reflection of axonal recruitment capacity.

summaries.beginner: Big-picture brain scans show networks rewiring after injury, but it is unlikely that brand-new long cables grow in adults. This review asks whether existing, highly branched axons—some barely making synapses—could be used to recruit extra brain areas instead.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2026; published April, 27(4):243–259), Richards, Huang, Bauer, and Lee review long-range axon branching as a candidate mechanism of network plasticity and repair. EM connectomes and projectomes from flies to humans show extreme arborization, differentially myelinated sister branches, and axonal regions nearly devoid of synapses. The authors consider whether those features, apparently evolutionarily conserved, enable large-scale functional remodeling after focal injury without new long-distance growth. They distinguish local synaptic/sprouting plasticity from poorly understood long-range reintegration of damaged circuits into global networks.
summaries.advanced: This is a review/hypothesis paper, not a new reconstruction. Conservation of axonal features is attributed to “recent electron microscopic data.” Silent-branch persistence versus developmental pruning is explicitly unsolved. Clinical recovery speculation is not a trial result. Catalog method lists electron microscopy; the article synthesizes many studies.

plain_language_summary: Big-picture brain scans show networks rewiring after injury, but it is unlikely that brand-new long cables grow in adults. This review asks whether existing, highly branched axons—some barely making synapses—could be used to recruit extra brain areas instead.

ocar.opportunity: Many animals have proprioceptors that fire near joint limits, but what those signals do in a complete sensorimotor circuit—especially in a walking animal with a connectome—was poorly specified.
ocar.challenge: In vertebrates, joint-capsule receptors are less understood downstream than muscle spindles; in insects, hair-plate function and wiring to motor neurons needed combined physiology, EM reconstruction, and causal tests.
ocar.action: In Nature Communications (2026), Pratt, Dallmann, Chou, Siwanowicz, Tuthill and colleagues study Drosophila coxal hair plate CxHP8 with calcium imaging in behaving flies, reconstruct its axons in an EM dataset, optogenetically activate and silence it, then generalize by reconstructing other leg hair plates’ morphology and downstream connectivity.
ocar.resolution: CxHP8 detects limits of anterior leg movement and is wired to excite posterior and inhibit anterior motor output. Activation elicits posterior postural reflexes; silencing alters the swing-to-stance transition. They conclude each hair plate is specialized for reflexes matched to the joint limit it detects, illustrating prediction of sensorimotor reflexes from a connectome with identified proprioceptors and motor neurons.
ocar.future_work: Predictions for other hair plates from anatomy and connectivity remain to be fully tested in behaving animals; the paper presents CxHP8 as the worked example.

summaries.beginner: Flies have tiny hair sensors that fire when a leg is about to go too far. This study shows one hip-joint sensor both feels a forward stretch and is wired to pull the leg back, and it uses the fly nerve-cord wiring map to guess what the other hair sensors do.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Communications (2026), Pratt, Dallmann, Chou, Siwanowicz, Walling-Bell, Cook, Sustar, Azevedo, and Tuthill analyze hair-plate proprioceptors on the Drosophila leg. Calcium imaging shows CxHP8 encodes anterior movement limits. EM reconstruction indicates connectivity that would excite posterior and inhibit anterior motor neurons. Optogenetic activation produces posterior postural reflexes; silencing changes walking’s swing-to-stance transition. Comprehensive peripheral and downstream reconstructions are used to predict functions of other hair plates as limit-matched reflex specialists.
summaries.advanced: Causal tests in the abstract are strongest for CxHP8; other hair plates are predictions from morphology and connectivity. The EM dataset is “an electron microscopy dataset,” not named in the abstract. Catalog organism is fly; this is adult leg/VNC sensorimotor work, not a brain connectome paper.

plain_language_summary: Flies have tiny hair sensors that fire when a leg is about to go too far. This study shows one hip-joint sensor both feels a forward stretch and is wired to pull the leg back, and it uses the fly nerve-cord wiring map to guess what the other hair sensors do.

ocar.opportunity: Dense EM connectomes of the Drosophila early olfactory system now visualize every cell type, neuron, and synapse along a pathway that has long been a model for olfactory processing and associative memory.
ocar.challenge: A complete wiring diagram still does not reveal functional logic: the classic feedforward sketch hides dense local feedback among large multi-input multi-output neurons, and there is no agreed quantitative account of natural odorants that the circuit must classify.
ocar.action: Lazar and Zhou review fifteen years of EOS connectome and synaptome datasets, emphasizing feedback-loop abstractions that govern input/output transformations at each neuropil, plus the need for an odorant-object model of the environment and causal, real-time treatment of the pathway as cascaded giant local feedback loops.
ocar.resolution: They argue that systematic understanding of those feedback abstractions is the foundation of EOS functional logic, and that odor semantics/syntax require new distance measures for classifying odorant objects in support of associative memory.
ocar.future_work: The paper sets an agenda for models that respect causality and environmental statistics rather than delivering a new reconstruction or fitted odor-space metric.

summaries.beginner: Having a complete wiring diagram of the fly’s early smell circuit is not the same as knowing how smell works. This essay argues that local feedback loops and a model of real-world odors are what turn the map into a theory of computation.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2026 article, Lazar and Zhou review Drosophila early-olfactory-system connectomes and synaptomes. They note that a well-characterized feedforward path into associative memory is embedded in dense local feedback of large MIMO neurons. Functional logic, they argue, depends on abstractions of those feedback loops at each neuropil, on an explicit generative model of environmental odorant objects (semantics and syntax), and on treating the circuit as a causal real-time cascade rather than a static graph. New distance measures for odorant classification are called for.
summaries.advanced: The attached PDF extract does not match this catalog record: it is Coons and Zucal on Markov bases for Forman-Ricci curvature of graphs (arXiv:2608.01929). Summaries follow the EOS review abstract only. No synapse counts or named EM volumes appear in that abstract. Journal field is empty in the catalog row.

plain_language_summary: Having a complete wiring diagram of the fly’s early smell circuit is not the same as knowing how smell works. This essay argues that local feedback loops and a model of real-world odors are what turn the map into a theory of computation.

ocar.opportunity: Nervous systems communicate by fast synaptic wires and slower diffusive extrasynaptic signals, but how those modes jointly organize function is unclear even when both maps exist.
ocar.challenge: Anatomical synapses do not fully determine influence: neurons can act at a distance, and comparing a neuropeptide network to wiring requires a shared functional language rather than overlaying two graphs.
ocar.action: In a 2026 arXiv-style paper (dated 3 April 2026), Sunil, Benali, and Moutuou infer structure-derived functional connectivity on the C. elegans synaptic connectome from equilibrium statistical-physics principles, then compare that probabilistic flow map with the complete neuropeptidergic extrasynaptic connectome in a multiplex framework.
ocar.resolution: They report four complementary regimes: (i) topology-dependent extrasynaptic signaling that reinforces synaptic motor circuits; (ii) a topology-resilient modulatory layer for global regulation and behavioral state; (iii) a purely extrasynaptic network for survival and homeostasis; (iv) a purely synaptic regime for rapid sensorimotor processing. Examples in supplements include sparsely wired but extrasynaptically rich neurons (CAN, M4) versus high-degree synaptic subgraph cells (RME, PHC, AS10, FLP).
ocar.future_work: They offer the multiplex comparison as a general strategy for other species’ structural and modulatory connectomes; experimental perturbation of the four regimes is not the result here.

summaries.beginner: Worms talk both through wired synapses and through slower chemical broadcasts. This study puts both maps in one framework and argues each mode is tuned for a different job: fast reflexes, motor stability, whole-body states, or staying alive.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2026 theoretical/computational paper, Sunil, Benali, and Moutuou combine the complete C. elegans synaptic and neuropeptidergic connectomes. Functional connectivity is inferred from the synaptic graph using equilibrium statistical physics, then compared with extrasynaptic peptide wiring. Four communication regimes emerge, specialized for speed, modulation, robustness, and survival. Significance text stresses that extrasynaptic signaling is structured, not a blurry extension of synapses.
summaries.advanced: “Complete” refers to published worm synaptic and neuropeptide maps they analyze, not a new EM volume. Functional connectivity is structure-derived and probabilistic, not recorded activity. Four-regime labels are their interpretive partition. Journal/DOI fields are empty; the extract is an arXiv PDF (2604.02057).

plain_language_summary: Worms talk both through wired synapses and through slower chemical broadcasts. This study puts both maps in one framework and argues each mode is tuned for a different job: fast reflexes, motor stability, whole-body states, or staying alive.

ocar.opportunity: Connectome mapping still depends on manual correction of automated tracing errors; at mouse-brain scale that proofreading has been estimated to dominate cost (Jefferis et al. 2023: billions of dollars, over 90% of a project budget if current methods were used).
ocar.challenge: Even millimeter-scale reconstructions leave error-free path lengths on the order of a millimeter, while real processes are much longer; Drosophila projects already consumed tens of person-years of proofreading for one insect brain.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv (2025), Januszewski, Templier, Hayworth, Peale, and Hess introduce PATHFINDER: an AI system that segments volumes, proposes assemblies of neuron fragments, and scores shape plausibility, trained from sparse fully traced neurites rather than by imitating human clicks, and evaluated on all axons in an IBEAM-mSEM mouse-cortex volume.
ocar.resolution: They report an order-of-magnitude reduction in axon reconstruction error versus previous state of the art (simultaneous split and merge improvement versus Schmidt et al. 2024) and up to 84× proofreading-throughput improvement relative to prior whole-mouse-brain estimates. Evaluation path length is two orders of magnitude larger than Januszewski et al. 2018 and Schmidt et al. 2024. They argue proofreading cost can become comparable to acquisition at mouse-brain scale.
ocar.future_work: They anticipate wider fields of view with more data, image features, self-supervised pretraining, and equivariant representations. Ground truth could later come from CLEM or LICONN instead of manual traces. PATHFINDER is positioned as complementary to auto-proofreading heuristics, not a replacement for all human review.

summaries.beginner: Tracing every axon in a mouse brain by hand would take forever and cost a fortune. This AI system glues axon pieces together by judging which shapes look like real neurons, and the authors say it makes far fewer mistakes than earlier automatic tracers.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2025 bioRxiv preprint, Januszewski (Google Research) and Hess lab colleagues present PATHFINDER for neuron reconstruction. The system segments, enumerates fragment assemblies, and evaluates morphological plausibility. On all axons in an IBEAM-mSEM mouse cortical volume, axon error rates drop by an order of magnitude versus recent SOTA, with claimed proofreading throughput gains up to 84× versus prior whole-mouse-brain estimates. Human tracing is cited at about 1 mm/h even with optimized tools (Boergens et al. 2017). They evaluate on the full axonal set to avoid subset bias.
summaries.advanced: “Up to 84×” is relative to prior whole-mouse-brain proofreading estimates, not a timed user study in this extract. Order-of-magnitude split and merge gains are versus Schmidt et al. 2024 as stated. Completeness of connectivity matrices is explicitly less than full. IBEAM-mSEM mouse cortex is the test domain; fly-scale person-year figures are background. OCR artifacts appear in the PDF extract (arrows for ×).

plain_language_summary: Tracing every axon in a mouse brain by hand would take forever and cost a fortune. This AI system glues axon pieces together by judging which shapes look like real neurons, and the authors say it makes far fewer mistakes than earlier automatic tracers.

ocar.opportunity: In mouse V1, excitatory neurons with similar responses are more likely to connect, but whether that like-to-like rule holds across layers, areas, and feedback, and whether it is more than axon–dendrite proximity, was open at millimeter scale.
ocar.challenge: Separating feature tuning from receptive-field location, and asking about higher-order structure among a cell’s postsynaptic cohort, requires jointly measured function and synapses across a large volume.
ocar.action: In Nature (2025), Ding, Fahey, Papadopoulos, Tolias, Reimer and the MICrONS consortium analyze synaptic connectivity and visual responses in the millimeter-scale MICrONS mouse visual-cortex dataset, using a validated digital-twin model to split feature versus spatial tuning, then train recurrent nets on a classification task and ablate like-to-like weights.
ocar.resolution: Like-to-like connectivity appears within and across layers and areas, including feedback, and only the feature component of tuning predicts fine-scale synapses beyond geometric proximity. Postsynaptic cohorts are more functionally similar than pairwise like-to-like predicts. RNNs develop similar pairwise and higher-order patterns, and ablating like-to-like connections hurts task performance more than ablating random ones.
ocar.future_work: They suggest these rules may matter for sensory processing and learning in both biological and artificial systems; whether they hold outside visual cortex is not shown here.

summaries.beginner: Brain cells that like the same pictures tend to wire to each other, not just next door but across visual areas. This mouse study finds that pattern in a cubic-millimeter wiring-and-activity map, and a simple artificial network grows the same habit when trained to classify.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2025), Ding, Fahey, Papadopoulos and colleagues use the MICrONS millimeter-scale mouse visual cortex dataset. Neurons with similar response properties connect preferentially within and across layers and areas, including feedback, supporting a general like-to-like rule in the visual hierarchy. A digital twin decomposes tuning into feature and spatial parts; only feature similarity predicts fine-scale synapses beyond axon–dendrite proximity. A higher-order rule is that postsynaptic cohorts of a given presynaptic cell are more similar than pairwise statistics predict. RNNs trained on classification spontaneously acquire both rules; targeted ablation of like-to-like weights impairs performance more than random ablation.
summaries.advanced: Functional analyses use MICrONS plus additional two-photon experiments in ten mice (3 female, 7 male, 78–190 days) of Slc17a7-Cre;Ai162 background; MICrONS itself is from one 75-day-old male of the same strain. Sex-disaggregated analysis was not performed because of sample size. “Magnitudes similar” to MICrONS in RNNs is the authors’ comparison. Like-to-like is reported for the excitatory/visual-hierarchy setting they analyze, not all cell classes.

plain_language_summary: Brain cells that like the same pictures tend to wire to each other, not just next door but across visual areas. This mouse study finds that pattern in a cubic-millimeter wiring-and-activity map, and a simple artificial network grows the same habit when trained to classify.

ocar.opportunity: Millimeter-scale cortical EM volumes contain tens of thousands of cells, most incompletely reconstructed, so cell typing cannot wait for full arbors.
ocar.challenge: Proofreading-sensitive morphological graphs and methods that need complete dendrites cover less than half the cells and cannot stably label truncated neurons or rare types.
ocar.action: In Nature (2025), Elabbady, Seshamani, Mu, Collman and the MICrONS team survey quantitative perisomatic ultrastructure of nearly 100,000 cells in a cubic millimetre of mouse visual cortex, showing that soma-neighborhood features classify types including connectivity-defined types, then use those labels to characterize cell-type-specific wiring and to hunt rare motifs.
ocar.resolution: Perisomatic features suffice to identify cell types dataset-wide in a way that is relatively insensitive to proofreading and truncation. The classifier has already supported studies of layer 5 Martinotti cells, 5P-ET motifs, and interneurons outside a manually labeled column. It is fast and computationally inexpensive relative to whole-arbor methods.
ocar.future_work: They note greater inhibitory diversity than in the labeled column, unused somatic image detail (organelles, embeddings), and possible extension to glia (for example OPC versus premyelinating oligodendrocytes) and to X-ray or light-microscopy somatic measurements.

summaries.beginner: In a huge electron-microscope block of mouse cortex, most cells are only partly traced, so naming them from their full shape is impossible. This paper shows that measurements around the cell body are enough to assign types and to find rare wiring patterns.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2025; received 2023, accepted June 2024, published 9 April 2025), Elabbady and colleagues classify nearly 100,000 cells in the MICrONS cubic-millimetre mouse cortical volume from perisomatic EM features. They argue this is sufficient even for types defined mainly by connectivity, enabling dataset-wide, proofreading-robust labels and targeted proofreading of rare patterns. Compared with morphology-graph methods restricted to high-quality reconstructions, coverage is much broader. Applications already include L5 Martinotti connectivity, 5P-ET inhibitory motifs, and interneurons outside the expert-labeled column.
summaries.advanced: “Tens of thousands of neurons” in the opening versus “nearly 100,000 cells” includes non-neuronal somata in the survey. Validation is described as consistent with more inhibitory diversity than the column labels capture. The model does not use all somatic ultrastructure or extra-somatic local features (neurotransmitter identity, cilia, and so on) that other work has used. Catalog year 2025 matches the Nature publication.

plain_language_summary: In a huge electron-microscope block of mouse cortex, most cells are only partly traced, so naming them from their full shape is impossible. This paper shows that measurements around the cell body are enough to assign types and to find rare wiring patterns.

ocar.opportunity: Different Drosophila EM reconstructions of similar circuitry report different synapse counts, which matters for comparing connectomes across labs and techniques.
ocar.challenge: Sample size, software detectors, proofreading, sex, age, and imaging modality (ssTEM versus FIB-SEM) are confounded; raw counts cannot be compared naively.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv (2025), Scheffer estimates human-visible synapse numbers from raw detections in FANC, MANC, FAFB (original and FAFB2), male CNS, BANC, hemibrain, and smaller optic-lobe volumes, compensating where possible for volume and detector efficiency, then compares overlapping compartments pairwise.
ocar.resolution: In almost all known cases reconstructed by both techniques, isotropic FIB-SEM volumes show more human-visible synapses than microtome-sliced ssTEM, typically by more than 40%. He interprets this as strong but not conclusive evidence that synapses are easier to see in isotropic FIB-SEM.
ocar.future_work: If anisotropy is the issue, better human ground truth and possibly machine detection of subtle cues (by analogy to neurotransmitter prediction) are suggested. Tables of path-strength reporting (for example ≥5-synapse “strong” paths) illustrate how count differences propagate into graph statistics.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly wiring maps from different microscopes do not agree on how many synapses they see. This comparison finds that 3D ion-beam microscopes usually show over 40% more human-visible synapses than sliced transmission-EM volumes of matching regions.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2025 bioRxiv preprint, Louis Scheffer compares synapse detection across major Drosophila reconstructions (1C, 7C, FIB19, hemibrain, FANC, FAFB/FAFB2, MANC, male CNS, BANC, and others). Analyses use raw synapse counts to avoid proofreading dependence and attempt to correct for sample size and software efficiency, estimating synapses a skilled human would see. Pairwise comparison of overlapping regions finds FIB-SEM typically exceeding ssTEM by more than 40% in human-visible synapses. The conclusion is carefully hedged: strongly suggestive, not proven.
summaries.advanced: “Typically by more than 40%” is the headline comparison, not a single universal factor. Confounds of genotype, age, and true biological variation remain. FAFB2 is a new synapse set on ssTEM, not a new volume. Table 8 in the extract reports odds that paths of given biological strength are called strong (≥5 synapses) across BANC, FAFB, hemibrain, CNS, and MANC—those percentages are graph-threshold statistics, not the 40% imaging result.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly wiring maps from different microscopes do not agree on how many synapses they see. This comparison finds that 3D ion-beam microscopes usually show over 40% more human-visible synapses than sliced transmission-EM volumes of matching regions.

ocar.opportunity: Cell-type-specific genetic access is required for functional, transcriptomic, and proteomic work in Drosophila, and split-GAL4 lines can target identified types if a large, curated collection exists and can be linked to EM connectomes.
ocar.challenge: Generating specific drivers means screening vast hemidriver combinations, validating expression, and coping with residual off-target labeling; many types still lack a precise line.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv (2024), Meissner, the FlyLight Project Team, Rubin and colleagues describe collections of 3063 split-GAL4 lines targeting adult CNS cell types and 1020 lines characterized in third-instar larvae, from screening over 77,000 hemidriver combinations, with NeuronBridge linking light-microscopy images to EM reconstructions, plus 300,000 new 3D images of other split combinations.
ocar.resolution: The resource enables anatomy-based choice of existing or new hemidriver pairs. Discussion notes FlyLight’s broader image corpus (540,000 3D images from 230,000 GAL4/LexA/split samples) and stock distribution. They estimate, as a rule of thumb, precise lines for about one third of CNS cell types, imprecise lines for another third, and no usable line for the rest with this enhancer-fragment strategy.
ocar.future_work: Complete coverage would need other enhancer-capture strategies and further intersectional restriction (GAL80, Flp, killer zipper). Users should validate multiple lines, effectors, insertion sites, and fly age. Peripheral nervous system and the body were out of scope.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly neuroscientists need genetic switches that turn on in just one kind of nerve cell. This huge collection of split-GAL4 fly stocks, with pictures matched to electron-microscope maps, makes it much easier to grab the cell type you want.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2024 bioRxiv preprint, Meissner, Aso, Card, Dickson, Korff, Ito, Truman, Zlatic, Rubin, and the Janelia FlyLight team release 3063 adult and 1020 larval split-GAL4 lines after screening more than 77,000 hemidriver combinations. NeuronBridge and related tools connect these light-level patterns to EM connectomes. An additional 300,000 3D images of other split-GAL4 combinations are made searchable. The authors stress residual off-target expression, the need to confirm results with multiple lines, and incomplete CNS coverage with Generation-1 enhancer fragments.
summaries.advanced: The catalog abstract lists 3060 adult and 1373 larval lines; the PDF abstract used here lists 3063 and 1020—follow the PDF. The one-third/one-third/one-third coverage split is an explicit rule of thumb, not a census. “Well-characterized” still includes lines with some off-target expression (their Figure 2, not shown in the extract).

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly neuroscientists need genetic switches that turn on in just one kind of nerve cell. This huge collection of split-GAL4 fly stocks, with pictures matched to electron-microscope maps, makes it much easier to grab the cell type you want.

ocar.opportunity: X-ray holographic nanotomography can resolve subcellular detail across ~mm³ landscapes of intact tissue and is compatible with follow-up volume EM, offering cell-density and spatial-distribution maps that histology needs for circuit and tissue mechanics.
ocar.challenge: Manual annotation of nuclei in terabyte-scale ~mm³ volumes is unrealistic; classifiers must generalize across biological replicates with little extra ground truth and support multi-user proofreading.
ocar.action: In SPIE Optical Engineering + Applications (2024), Nathansen, Clausen, Berning, Bosch, Rzepka and colleagues train an automated nuclei segmenter for mouse-brain XNH, run it on HPC, and export a data table plus browser-explorable segmentations and meshes (WEBKNOSSOS) for collaborative proofreading.
ocar.resolution: The classifier reports spatial locations and morphologies of about 80,000 nuclei per dataset with high recall, generalizes to similar replicate datasets with minimal added ground truth, and is positioned for automated histological pipelines in systems neuroscience and broader tissue biology. Meshes larger than 10× mean nuclear volume were treated as conversion artefacts and masked.
ocar.future_work: Code and training data are on GitHub (cboschp/segVolData). Conflicts: several authors are at scalable minds, which sells related software. Broader tissue types beyond mouse brain XNH are a stated use, not the training domain.

summaries.beginner: A new X-ray microscope can photograph a cubic millimetre of mouse brain in enough detail to see cell nuclei, but there are tens of thousands of them. This paper trains a computer to find those nuclei and puts the results in a browser so people can check the work.
summaries.intermediate: In Proc. SPIE 13152 (2024), Nathansen, Clausen, Berning, MacKenzie, Zhang, Pacureanu, Schaefer, Rzepka, and Bosch segment cell nuclei in mm-scale mouse-brain X-ray holographic nanotomography. Manual labeling is treated as infeasible at ~mm³ / terabyte scale. The automated classifier yields ~80k nuclei per dataset with high recall, transfers to biological replicates with little extra ground truth, and emits tables plus WEBKNOSSOS meshes. XNH is motivated as nondestructive and EM-compatible. Precision/recall are averaged across subvolumes (their Table 1, not numeric in the extract).
summaries.advanced: “High recall” is qualitative in the abstract; Table 1 numbers are not in the selected text. ~80k is per dataset. Catalog lists MICrONS among datasets; the paper itself is XNH mouse brain, not the MICrONS EM volume. Nuclei with volume >10× the mean were excluded as artefacts. Commercial affiliations are disclosed.

plain_language_summary: A new X-ray microscope can photograph a cubic millimetre of mouse brain in enough detail to see cell nuclei, but there are tens of thousands of them. This paper trains a computer to find those nuclei and puts the results in a browser so people can check the work.

ocar.opportunity: Updated chemical and gap-junction connectomes of both adult C. elegans sexes now cover the whole animal including muscle and other end organs, so neuron functions and overall architecture can be read from connectivity rather than from the classic partial diagrams alone.
ocar.challenge: Despite decades of anatomy, circuits for behavior remain incomplete and many neuron classes still have unknown function; modular structure and the role of muscle as both sink and sensory source were under-emphasized.
ocar.action: In PLoS Biology (2024), Emmons applies modularity analysis and degree-based inspection to these whole-animal connectomes to partition communities, highlight end-organ convergence/feedback, and propose functions for previously unstudied neurons.
ocar.resolution: Ten communities map onto broad behavioral categories. Body-wall muscle is both a major convergence site and, via a body-wide mechanosensory field onto DVA and PVR, a feedback source; most interneurons have similar in- and out-degree, dispersing information as much as they aggregate it. Newly emphasized features include high-degree gap-junction interneurons in the ventral cord and hub-and-spoke cells such as RIG and RMG.
ocar.future_work: The paper is offered as a guide for theory and for experiments on individual classes and circuits, not as a substitute for those experiments.
