summaries.beginner: The worm’s complete wiring list has been updated to include muscles and both sexes, but many cells still had no known job. This analysis splits the network into ten behavior-related groups and points to overlooked cells—including two that collect touch from the whole body.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS Biology (2024), Scott Emmons analyzes recently completed hermaphrodite and male C. elegans chemical and gap-junction connectomes including end organs. Modularity yields 10 communities correlated with behavioral categories. Muscle is both a hierarchical sink and, through a body-wide mechanosensory field onto DVA and PVR, a source of feedback. Multisensory integration is distributed: interneurons typically have matched in- and out-degree. Newly emphasized features include ventral-cord high-degree gap-junction interneurons and hub-and-spoke cells RIG and RMG. Several pathways involve previously unstudied neurons.
summaries.advanced: Community–behavior correlations and “suggested functions” are connectivity inferences, not new activity data. DVA/PVR as a body-wide field is an anatomical claim from convergence patterns. Analysis uses previously published connectome tables (author’s and others’); no new EM is reported. Sex differences are in the data but the abstract emphasizes shared architectural themes.

plain_language_summary: The worm’s complete wiring list has been updated to include muscles and both sexes, but many cells still had no known job. This analysis splits the network into ten behavior-related groups and points to overlooked cells—including two that collect touch from the whole body.

ocar.opportunity: Neurons mix receptor subtypes and receive mixed transmitters, so a connectome of partners is incomplete without knowing which neurotransmitter receptors sit at which identified synapses.
ocar.challenge: Localizing endogenous receptor subunits to specific inputs in single cells has been difficult without destroying native expression timing or lacking EM-identified partners.
ocar.action: In Neuron (2024), Sanfilippo, Kim, Bhukel, Aso, Zipursky and colleagues conditionally epitope-tag endogenous Drosophila neurotransmitter-receptor subunits, image them with expansion light-sheet microscopy, match synapses to EM connectomes, and immunopurify associated proteins, focusing on direction-selective T4/T5 motion-sensitive neurons.
ocar.resolution: Different receptor subunits occupy a stereotyped molecular topography aligned with cell-type-specific input domains, and developmental observations suggest receptors or receptor–membrane-protein complexes help determine input patterns. They identify a transmembrane protein restricted to a subset of spatially confined synapses and show genetically that it is required for synapse formation. They propose receptor spatial distribution as molecular cartography for dendritic connection patterns.
ocar.future_work: Tagged receptors are offered as a resource for localization, assembly, and plasticity studies. Concordance with EM is receptor-dependent (GluClα matches well; Rdl and nAChR subunits vary, possibly extrasynaptic or trafficking pools). Tagging other receptor classes will need structure-guided insertion sites.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram says who talks to whom, but not which molecular “mailbox” sits at each contact. This fly study tags native transmitter receptors, looks at them in super-resolution, and shows that different mailboxes sit in different neighborhoods on motion-detecting cells.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuron (2024; 112:942–958.e13), Sanfilippo et al. combine CRISPR tagging of endogenous cys-loop receptor subunits, expansion light-sheet microscopy, proteomics, and EM connectomics in Drosophila. In T4/T5 direction-selective neurons, multiple neurotransmitter receptors form stereotyped domain maps matched to cell-type-specific inputs. A transmembrane protein co-localizes with a spatially restricted synapse subset and is required for those synapses. The authors argue that targeting receptors to dendritic domains can specify wiring. Tags were inserted in poorly conserved cytoplasmic loops and still matched presynaptic Brp/Cac and expected transmitters.
summaries.advanced: Not all receptor puncta equal EM synapses: extrasynaptic or trafficking receptors may inflate counts (Rdl). Requirement of the identified transmembrane protein is genetic evidence for a subset of synapses, not all inputs. Catalog method lists light-sheet; EM is used for partner identity. This is fly visual motion circuitry, not a brain-wide receptor atlas.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram says who talks to whom, but not which molecular “mailbox” sits at each contact. This fly study tags native transmitter receptors, looks at them in super-resolution, and shows that different mailboxes sit in different neighborhoods on motion-detecting cells.

ocar.opportunity: Neuropeptides are abundant, diverse modulators of physiology and behavior; C. elegans, with a compact nervous system and a mapped synaptic connectome, is a prototype for organism-wide peptide networks.
ocar.challenge: Organization of peptide–receptor pathways, circuit motifs, and the spatial/temporal range of extrasynaptic transmission needed a synthesis spanning conservation, expression, ligand–receptor maps, and in vivo function.
ocar.action: In a Genetics (2024) WormBook-style review, Watteyne, Chudinova, Ripoll-Sánchez, Schafer, and Beets survey evolutionary conservation, molecular expression, receptor–ligand pairing, and system-wide architecture of C. elegans neuropeptide signaling, plus motifs and timescales from in vivo studies.
ocar.resolution: They describe an extensive extrasynaptic network whose structure differs from synaptic and monoamine graphs, with combinatorial convergent, antagonistic, feedforward, and feedback peptide actions spanning seconds (NLP-40 on DVB/defecation) to minutes (PDF-1 versus serotonin roaming/dwelling) to hours (FLP-1 pathogen avoidance). Whole-brain imaging (Randi et al. 2023) indicates extrasynaptic signaling also shapes short-timescale dynamics. They position the worm peptidergic connectome as a prototype for other species.
ocar.future_work: How coexpression fingerprints translate into addressed communication in pervasive peptide networks remains open, as does transferring motifs to vertebrates even though broad peptide/receptor coexpression is already reported there.

summaries.beginner: Besides wired synapses, worm neurons broadcast many small peptides that change behavior over seconds to hours. This review maps that chemical network and explains the repeating circuit tricks—push, pull, loops—that peptides use.
summaries.intermediate: In Genetics (2024), Watteyne, Chudinova, Ripoll-Sánchez, Schafer, and Beets review the C. elegans neuropeptide signaling network. Recent maps of expression, ligand–receptor interactions, and system-wide organization, together with in vivo circuit studies, show a combinatorial extrasynaptic web distinct from chemical-synapse and monoamine networks. Examples include PDF-1/serotonin antagonism of roaming versus dwelling on a minutes scale, FLP-1 effects including hours-long pathogen avoidance, and second-scale NLP-40 control of defecation via DVB. Functional-connectivity imaging suggests broad short-timescale extrasynaptic impact. The worm is offered as a prototype while peptide mapping proceeds in other animals.
summaries.advanced: This is a review; no new connectome is generated (data-availability statement: no new data). Specific motif examples are drawn from cited studies. “Prototype” is a framing claim. Catalog dataset is the White+ C. elegans connectome used as context, not the peptide map itself.

plain_language_summary: Besides wired synapses, worm neurons broadcast many small peptides that change behavior over seconds to hours. This review maps that chemical network and explains the repeating circuit tricks—push, pull, loops—that peptides use.

ocar.opportunity: A complete adult male Drosophila ventral-nerve-cord connectome (MANC; companion Takemura et al., 2023) is the first synaptic-resolution nerve cord of an animal that walks and flies, but it is unusable without systematic names linking cells to the experimental literature.
ocar.challenge: A century of VNC work focused on accessible neurons, leaving most interneurons a black box; hemilineage studies helped, but a full inventory, serial homology, sensory modalities, and programmatic types were missing.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv (2024 posting of a 2023 manuscript), Marin, Morris, Stürner, Jefferis and colleagues apply hierarchical annotations, group neurons across midline and segments, define systematic types for sensory, intrinsic, ascending, and non-motor efferent neurons, assign hemilineages and neurotransmitters, and release annotations in neuPrint and Clio.
ocar.resolution: They classify 13,060 VNC intrinsics, 185 ascending, 1,328 descending, 737 motor, about 100 other efferent, and nearly 6,500 sensory neurons, assigning hemilineages to 88% of VNC neurons (97% of thoracic-origin cells). Over 35% of intrinsic, ascending, and non-motor efferent neurons match across segments, and sensory modality is assigned to over 5,000 sensory neurons, revealing serial types and a layered organization likely matching the periphery. Larval-born neurons in a hemilineage usually share a transmitter, though earlier-born neurons often differ; the annotations underpin descending-input and motor-output analyses in a companion paper (Cheong et al., 2023).
ocar.future_work: They did not match every published light-level type; experts must still bridge most cells to images. Serial homology covers over a third of non-descending, non-sensory neurons, not all. Primary-neuron counts slightly exceed some larval estimates, pending a complete larval VNC tabulation.

summaries.beginner: A complete wiring diagram of a male fruit-fly nerve cord is only useful if every cell has a name and a job description. This companion paper labels tens of thousands of neurons, matches many of them across body segments, and posts the phone book next to the map.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2024 bioRxiv companion to the MANC connectome, Marin et al. systematically annotate the adult male Drosophila VNC: 13,060 intrinsics, 185 ascending, 1,328 descending, 737 motor, about 100 other efferent, and nearly 6,500 sensory neurons. They assign hemilineages (88% of VNC neurons), soma side, neuromere, estimated birth time, neuropils, and subclasses, matching over 35% of intrinsic/ascending/non-motor-efferent neurons as serial sets. More than 5,000 sensory neurons receive a modality label; thoracic totals (T1 4,483; T2 5,080; T3 3,988 after 01B correction) closely match classical estimates of 4,100–5,000 neurons per neuromere. Annotations are released through neuPrint/Clio and programmatic tools.
summaries.advanced: MANC is male adult VNC; female FANC is a different dataset. Descending-neuron biology is deferred to the Cheong companion. 10.5% of thoracic neurons annotated primary exceeds some first-instar thoracic counts; the authors treat larval persistence as likely but not proven. “First complete nerve cord for an animal that can walk or fly” is the companion acquisition paper’s claim as cited here.

plain_language_summary: A complete wiring diagram of a male fruit-fly nerve cord is only useful if every cell has a name and a job description. This companion paper labels tens of thousands of neurons, matches many of them across body segments, and posts the phone book next to the map.
